page_placements.theme: Toy models: where superposition and polysemanticity come from, and their geometry

record.tranche_reason: The post studies incidental polysemanticity in a synthetic toy network, but does not test any of the listed versions about modern-model audits, InceptionV1, attribution graphs, or explanation scoring.
record.gate_note: The post derives an expected count of polysemantic neurons and reports toy-model experiments on that count. These results concern the topic but do not test the specific models or claims in V1–V7. The sparsification simulation measures l1 norm and nonzero coordinates, not polysemanticity, so it is not recorded as a row.
record.test_reason: A toy autoencoder study of how incidental polysemanticity arises when neurons outnumber features. It measures no language-model or InceptionV1 neuron audit, no attribution graphs and no explanation scoring, so its results do not bear on whether any of V1–V7 holds. It is related in theme only: an alternative origin of polysemanticity besides superposition, which touches V3/V4's framing.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue polysemanticity can arise incidentally, from random initialization amplified by winner-take-all dynamics, even with ample neurons. Their toy experiments match the predicted Θ(n²/m) count with constant about 1/4. They add that this type may need different remedies than superposition, such as nudging training rather than adding neurons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic autoencoder with basis-vector data, tied weights, and l1 activation regularization to study incidental polysemanticity; it does not use a modern-model neuron audit or explanation-testing procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported number of polysemantic neurons varies with hidden size m, following Θ(n²/m) in the tested toy-model sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: In a tied-weight ReLU autoencoder with l1 activation penalty, basis-vector data, n=256 and m=256–4096, polysemantic neurons still arise when m≥n. Their count follows roughly n²/(4m).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemanticity can arise incidentally from random initialization plus winner-take-all training dynamics, even without more features than neurons (toy setting).

record.problems: The evidence is from a deliberately simplified toy setup with basis-vector inputs and l1 activation regularization. The post says the full interaction of training forces is not yet theoretically understood and identifies questions about feature co-occurrence and other sources of winner-take-all dynamics for future work.
record.rows_left_out: The numerical simulation of sparsification is omitted because it reports l1 norm and estimated nonzero coordinates, not polysemanticity (Numerical simulations).

untested.parts: Other language models, dense and MoE, and scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, and recursive generalization.
Effects of architecture, regularization and tools on the interpretable share in real models. The post only speculates that training-trajectory nudges could remove incidental polysemanticity.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict where a neuron fires.

record.verdict_notes: Preliminary Alignment Forum post. In comments, Rohin Shah argues the result may be very sensitive to features never co-occurring, and the authors agree this is untested. Excluding the sparsification simulation from the rows is appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its reported shares of one-job, two-related-job, and not-yet-understood neuron poles.
Language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization, tools, and the stated interpretability estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict where a neuron fires on other examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
